abstract: Terrain-aware locomotion training requires fast simulation without sacrificing temporal experience. We keep Isaac Gym simulation and proximal policy optimization (PPO) on one GPU, reducing data transfers while collecting experience from thousands of robots. An adaptive curriculum promotes or demotes each robot according to traversal performance by relocating it among tiled terrain levels, changing difficulty without regenerating the shared mesh. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; training incorporates friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling for transfer. PPO uses large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping, but increasing robot count at fixed batch size shortens rollouts and can impair learning. On an i9-11900k workstation with an NVIDIA RTX A6000, ANYmal C training with 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates took under 20 minutes. Simulated crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for stair steps up to 0.2 m; obstacle success declined with difficulty, and slope climbing failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy traversed stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, but imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness, prompting a 0.6 m/s linear-velocity command limit. These experiments support rapid training and deployment under the tested temporal, terrain, and sensing conditions.
methods: In proximal policy optimization (PPO), the critic estimates an infinite-horizon discounted return. A failure or goal completion is a task termination the critic can anticipate. A time limit, however, interrupts a continuing task without an observable warning: episode time is absent from the observations. Treating this reset like a failure would remove the continuation value from the target, even though the task did not end for a predictable reason. The modified environment interface therefore identifies time-outs separately. For these transitions, the reward is augmented with the critic's discounted estimate of remaining return, bootstrapping its target rather than assigning zero future return. This handling cannot assume that time-outs occur only at batch boundaries: episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches. Completing a collection batch does not reset the environment; time-limit resets must be detected wherever they occur.
results: Figure 4 supports a task-specific reward-time trade-off rather than unlimited scaling. To prevent curriculum-driven difficulty changes from confounding reward, the experiment reduces maximum stair and obstacle heights and trains without the curriculum. It reports total episode reward as mean and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, more robots mean fewer consecutive steps per robot: training time decreases, but reward drops sharply at excessive parallelism, consistent with inadequate temporal information for advantage estimation. Throughput gains also slow beyond roughly 4,000 robots. With fewer robots, reward declines more gradually; the authors suggest this reflects less diverse, correlated samples from longer trajectories. Larger batches yield higher reward and delay the high-parallelism drop, while increasing training time. The 20,000-robot baseline uses 50 steps per robot and one million samples per update; it achieves the highest reward at greater training cost, not under a matched sample budget. Thus, about 2,048-4,096 robots with approximately 100,000-200,000 samples per batch balance reward and time for this simplified task, subject to temporal-data requirements and throughput saturation.
notes: Revision decisions: the abstract links GPU residency to reduced copying and curriculum relocation to difficulty changes without rebuilding terrain; Methods links unobservable time-outs to continuation-value bootstrapping; Results links fixed-batch scaling to shorter rollouts, preserving both reward losses. Exact Figure 4 reward values, training times, and standard deviations are unavailable; none are reconstructed. The selected setup implies 24 rollout steps despite reported difficulty below 25; neither number is repaired or treated as a universal cutoff. Hardware demonstrations have no reported success rate. Other robot policies were retrained, with A1 and Cassie modifications; teacher-student integration remains future work.
